The analysis of the intact N-glycosylated fractions (Figure  A) showed that most peptide backbones were exclusively identified in different venoms, while only five were shared by all venoms. B. jararaca and B. insularis venoms showed the highest number of exclusive peptide sequences, respectively, 23 and 18, whereas in the other venoms around 30 exclusive peptide sequences were identified. Interestingly, peptides common to all venoms were restricted to four toxin classes: 5'-Nase, HYA, SVMP, and SVSP. Concerning the peptide identified in the nonglycosylated fractions (Figure  B), most were exclusively identified in only one venom, and all species shared only 50 sequences. The species with the highest number of exclusive peptides were B. jararaca and B. insularis, respectively, 245 and 234. Differently from the analysis of common peptide sequences of the intact N-glycosylated fractions, the 50 common peptides identified in the nonglycosylated fractions were derived from various toxin classes. Overall, both intersection profiles revealed a significant level of diversity between the venoms in both peptide backbone sets, adding to the notion that venom proteome variability is impacted by both amino acid sequence variations and occupation of the N-glycosylation sites.

The amino acid backbones of glycosylated peptides and nonglycosylated peptides were independently used to classify the venoms by hierarchical clustering (Figure S27) interestingly resulting in Bothrops venoms clustering according to their phylogenetic classification.
Discussion

This study builds upon our previous N-glycomic analysis of Bothrops venoms that revealed N-glycans characterized by different degrees of branching, isomer structures, and variable abundances, contributing to the complexity of venom proteomes, and the suggestion that the subproteomes of glycoproteins reflect the phenotypic plasticity found in congeneric species indicating distinct molecular signatures for each venom. Here, N-glycosylation in proteins of seven Bothrops venoms was deeply explored by (i) the quantification of neutral sugars in the venoms, (ii) the evaluation of the presence of carbohydrate structures by blotting using five lectins of different specificities, and (iii) the application of high-throughput mass spectrometric approaches to identify N-glycosylation sites and their corresponding N-glycan compositions in tryptic peptides, resulting in the most extensive profiling of snake venom glycosylation so far.

We started this study by the evaluation of the molecular masses of venom proteins by gel electrophoresis, under reducing and nonreducing conditions, which revealed protein band differences likely due to variable glycosylation levels (Figure S1). Indeed, it has been shown that, after de-N-glycosylation, the protein profiles of Bothrops venoms are more similar than in their native forms.   Thus, the differences observed in the evaluation of venom protein molecular mass by gel electrophoresis in this and other studies may reflect distinct N-glycan compositions or differences in the presence/occupation of N-glycosylation sites.   On the other hand, some observed differences in the low molecular mass range, especially below 20 kDa, could be explained by the differential abundance of some low molecular mass venom components, including toxin classes that are not glycosylated, such as CTL and PLA2.

The evaluation of venom glycosylation levels by measuring the contents of neutral carbohydrates did not reveal significant differences between the Bothrops venoms, and the value obtained for B. jararaca venom agreed with a previous analysis of this venom by the same method (Figure S2). Although the method used does not allow for the quantification of all types of monosaccharides commonly found in proteins, the data can be used to estimate the overall venom protein glycosylation level. From the N-glycosylation perspective, the basic core contains mannose units that can be detected by the method used. In the case of O-glycosylation, galactose units are frequently present in O-glycans, which also ensures some detection. A noteworthy comparison that confirms that the quantification of neutral carbohydrates may be used as an estimate of protein glycosylation levels involves the venoms of Crotalus durissus sp., whose values are around three times lower than those found for B. jararaca venom and agree with the fact that, in comparison to Bothrops, the venoms of C. durissus sp. contain a very low content of glycosylated proteinases (SVMPs and SVSPs).

Further, the qualitative analysis by lectin blot allowed the comparison of the occurrence of some carbohydrate structures in the venoms, and the results agreed with our previous N-glycomic data. In the case of GNA lectin, which binds to mannose units, it was interesting to observe the similar pattern of recognition among the venoms in agreement with our identification of N-glycosylated peptides, most of which showed the presence of shared N-glycan compositions of the high-mannose type in eight toxin classes (SVMP, SVSP, LAAO, 5'-Nase, APase, PDE, PLB, and HYA) identified in all venoms (Figure S6). In contrast, the lectin PNA did not recognize glycoproteins in any Bothrops venom (Figure S7). However, this result is limited by the fact that sialic acids inhibit PNA binding, and this condition was not tested. Even though B. jararacussu and B. moojeni venoms showed a weakly stained band of approximately 13-14 kDa that cross-reacted with the lectin, it likely does not contain a glycoprotein, but could rather contain a PLA2, since it has been shown that this kind of toxin, although not glycosylated, may interact with lectins.   There are only a few members of the venom PLA2 class that are glycoproteins,   and none of them were found in Bothrops venoms. Interestingly, mammalian secreted PLA2s are recognized by receptors that contain C-type lectin domains.

The lectins MAA and SNA (Figures S3 and S4) revealed significant differences in the recognition of proteins, which allowed the classification of the venoms in two groups: #1 (B. alcatraz, B. cotiara, B. fonsecai, B. insularis, and B. jararaca) and #2 (B. jararacussu and B. moojeni). MAA is generally used to probe whether the linkage between the sialic acid and galactose units at the nonreducing end of glycan structures is alpha-2,3. Our previous Bothrops N-glycome analysis indicated that the sialic acid unit in the N-glycan antennae is linked by a alpha-2,3 linkage. On the other hand, the lectin SNA, which recognizes sialic acid linked to galactose residues by an alpha-2,6 linkage, showed no recognition of proteins in all venoms, a finding that would suggest the absence of this type of linkage in Bothrops venom glycans. Since the proteins of B. jararacussu and B. moojeni venoms were not recognized by both MAA and SNA lectins, probably because of the absence of a Gal unit in their N-glycan antennae, it was not possible to define the linkage in the glycans of these venoms in this study (Figures S3 and S4).

In the case of the DSA lectin, which recognizes the structure Gal-1,4-GlcNAc and the polysaccharide chitin, the venoms showed a profile of weakly stained bands, except for B. jararacussu and B. moojeni venoms that were strongly recognized (Figure S5). The unexpected weak recognition observed in the venoms of B. alcatraz, B. cotiara, B. fonsecai, B. insularis, and B. jararaca could be explained by the presence of a sialic acid dimer in the Gal-1,4-GlcNAc structure, which could impair the recognition of N-glycan chains by DSA. Regarding the venoms of B. jararacussu and B. moojeni, the antenna composition of all N-glycans previously identified was HexNAc-1,4-HexNAc. Even though the data did not allow the determination of the N-acetylhexosamine that composed the N-glycans, their identities were suggested based on an analysis of the N-glycans found in an SVSP of B. moojeni venom. In this way, the strong recognition of glycoproteins by DSA in these two venoms may indicate that some N-acetylhexosamine dimers could be formed by GlcNAc-GlcNAc instead of the predicted GalNAc-1,4-GlcNAc structure.

In the analysis of N-glycosylated peptides enriched in the intact glycopeptide fractions, the large set of precursor ions generated in the mass spectrometer was originated from various types of peptides. As we used TiO2 affinity chromatography to enrich glycopeptides, any other peptide with affinity might have been enriched and composed of our sample subjected to LC-MS/MS, and possibly, eventually, also phosphopeptides. Moreover, precursors of O-glycosylated peptides were certainly present in our glycopeptide-enriched samples, and these were not assigned since our database is composed of N-glycans. We indeed have attempted to explore O-glycans in snake venom toxins, but so far, no reliable results have been obtained. Nonetheless, considering that about half of the putative N-glycosylated peptides were identified as glycosylated in the intact glycopeptide analysis using our designated set of N-glycans, we acknowledge that as a reasonable identification rate, which ensued in the identification of 1,715 intact N-glycosylated peptides present in all putatively glycosylated toxin classes of seven venoms.

Concerning the features of the glycosylation process, variability originates from the number of occupied glycosylation sites and the glycan structures attached to them. In Bothrops venoms, the contribution of N-glycosylation in interspecies variability was evidenced by the different numbers of intact N-glycopeptides identified. Although the analysis of peptide backbones revealed a higher number in B. jararaca venom, B. jararacussu and B. moojeni venoms (Figure  ) showed the highest number of identified intact N-glycopeptides whereas B. fonsecai venom showed the lowest. Nevertheless, the numeric differences cannot be interpreted as differential glycosylation levels in the venom proteins and might rather be due to (i) differences in the number of proteins available in the protein database employed in the search and (ii) the lack of N-glycomic data of B. fonsecai venom. Further, variation in the N-glycan compositions may also have contributed to the differences in the identification of intact N-glycosylated peptides, as some compositions could have been favored or disfavored in the ionization and fragmentation processes of mass spectrometry.

In all venoms analyzed in this study, high-mannose and hybrid/complex-type N-glycans were identified in all toxin classes. Our analyses also revealed that, in general, there was a predominance of hybrid/complex type N-glycans, and most of them were sialylated and fucosylated. However, the number of sialic acid units per N-glycan composition showed remarkable differences between the venoms and toxin classes, especially in proteinases (Figures   and Figure S18).

In our study, the heterogeneity analysis revealed that, considering all toxin classes together, the venoms showed similar average of heterogeneity: approximately three N-glycoforms per N-glycosylation site (Table S26). However, considering each venom separately, it was evident that heterogeneity varied between the toxin classes, and despite the higher number of different polypeptide chains of SVMPs and SVMPs, some nonabundant components, such as LAAO, HYA, and DPase, showed the highest heterogeneity levels (Table S26).

Overall, our data suggest that in Bothrops venom, protein variability involves both peptide backbones and N-glycan chains. Even in the case of venoms with similar N-glycan repertoires, such as B. alcatraz, B. insularis, and B. jararaca, our results did not show complete overlap of N-glycan compositions and N-glycosylated peptides (Figures S14 and S15). Furthermore, the identified N-glycosylated peptide backbones also represented a variability factor, as some peptide sequences were not identified in closely related species (Figure S27).

The evolutionary history of snake venom toxins and their hypothetical ancestors reveals progressive alterations in the amino acid composition and structural characteristics with the generation of functionally diverse molecules. Based on our analyses, despite the notable variability of occupation of glycosylation sites in Bothrops venom proteins, we show that Bothrops venom glycoproteomes contain a core of components that define their framework, which is conserved upon evolution in parallel to other molecular markers that determine their phylogenetic classification, as viewed by the clustering of the seven species, according to glycopeptide backbone + glycan composition, or glycan composition, or peptide backbone (Figures   and  and S27). Therefore, paradoxically, Bothrops venom phenotypes are conserved and divergent, indicating that evolution and divergence in the venom composition among species might be related to evolutionary responses to diet, habitat, and predator-prey interactions and need further studies to be fully understood.

Another noteworthy aspect of Bothrops venom protein glycosylation is the fact that it is a PTM restricted to polypeptide chains that contain at least 230 amino acid residues, such as the SVSPs, P-II and P-III SVMPs, and some less abundant enzymes (LAAO, HYA, 5'-Nase among others). Polypeptide chains containing around 200 amino acids or less, such as P-I SVMP, CRISP, PLA2, and CTL, are either devoid of or contain only one putative N-glycosylation site (for example, a few P-I SVSPs). Besides the importance of N-glycosylation in proteins related to their biological functions, stability, solubility (especially for secreted proteins), and protection from proteolysis, this PTM is also crucial in the quality control of protein folding taking place in the endoplasmic reticulum, shaping the glycoproteome of eukaryotic cells.   N-glycan positioning and composition (glyco-code) determines lectin chaperone selection; thus, N-glycosylation is important for the fate of newly synthesized secretory proteins, such as the venom proteins in the venom gland, where a productive fold may take place, resulting in proteins successfully secreted, or incorrectly folded proteins may be routed for displacement from the endoplasmic reticulum and be headed for degradation. It is therefore intriguing the fact that abundant toxins, such as CTL and PLA2, are not putatively N-glycosylated, however, display refined molecular structures that are fundamental for their functional activities.

Snake venom intra- and interspecies variability has been explored from different perspectives. -   The hypotheses behind this phenomenon usually consider two main possibilities: the presence of specific toxins and the differential abundance of specific toxin classes in the venoms. Although N-glycosylation is a common PTM in snake toxins, the identification of glycosylation sites, the features of glycan chains attached to toxins, and their role in shaping venom phenotypes are poorly explored. Interestingly, our data revealed some insights into the contribution of N-glycosylation to proteoform generation in some toxin classes.

Based on the N-glycosylation sites identified in this study, all N-glycosylated toxin classes in Bothrops venoms are enzymes that were identified as mainly containing N-glycan compositions of the hybrid/complex type, most of which were sialylated and fucosylated. Considering the human plasma as a reference, as it is, similarly to the venom, composed of secreted proteins, a high sialylation level in proteins is a common feature between them, which could be related to the fact that most toxins have systemic targets and should be carried by the circulation system to act in distant organs in the prey organism. In plasma glycoproteins, the presence of noncaped Gal, GalNAc, and NeuAc-2,6-GalNAc at the nonreducing end of glycan chains is related to their uptake by the asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR) by parenchymal liver cells. These receptors are also present in rodents, which are natural prey of many snake species, and therefore, it is possible that snake toxins could be selected upon evolution to contain sialic acid units to increase their half-life and favor their systemic effects. Interestingly, human plasma and venom N-glycosylated proteins differ in that the latter, according to our results, seem to contain more core fucosylated N-glycans.   Core fucosylation is an important modification of the N-glycan core in eukaryotes, and our venom N-glycomic analysis suggested the presence of this modification in most N-glycan compositions of Bothrops venoms. Core fucosylation modifies the N-glycan conformation, supporting a different orientation of the alpha1,6-arm.

Another important point of analysis is whether venom protein N-glycosylation is toxin class-specific or whether different N-glycan chains might be shared by different toxin classes. Our data did not show any specific N-glycan distribution among the toxin classes, and apparently, in each venom, N-glycan compositions of high-mannose and hybrid/complex types are found in all N-glycosylated proteins.

Considering the venom production cycle, it has been recently described that in the venom gland, some cells are committed with the synthesis of some toxin families, instead of a general production of the venom components distributed among all gland cells. This finding can be also correlated to another study that revealed an asynchronous synthesis of different toxin classes during the venom production cycle. Concerning the venom glycoproteins, the N-glycosylation process involves nontemplate-driven pathways, and the factors that affect variability in the N-glycosylation sites are steric accessibility of sequons during the protein translation and traffic along the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi lumen, and availability of nucleotide sugar in these organelles.   Further, as the N-glycosylation process is primarily cell-type-specific, sharing of N-glycan structures by the venom glycoproteins is a more parsimonious process, resulting in an unspecific use of N-glycan chains in the different toxin classes.

Venoms of the Bothrops genus have been prospected by proteomic approaches,   and a previous study of seven species found a similar profile of their glycoproteomic phenotypes and phylogenetic classification. Regarding snake venom proteome complexity, considering the possible contribution of mRNA splicing as a factor for protein variability, the protein inference problem in proteomic analyses performed by the bottom-up approach, and the PTMs, particularly glycosylation, it is still not possible to accurately assess the number of proteins and proteoforms that compose viperid venom.

In general, proteomic studies of the venoms of the Bothrops genus, including this work, were performed using bottom-up approaches. Hence, here, the numbers of protein groups identified by the analysis of the peptide nonglycosylated fractions agree with those usually reported in other studies (Figure  ).   The differences in the number of protein groups identified in the different venoms could be explained by the database used in the spectra search, which does not contain similar contents of protein sequences of the analyzed species. Nevertheless, as expected, most toxins that were detected in all of the venoms were SVMPs and SVSPs.

A comparison of backbones identified in the intact N-glycopeptide and nonglycosylated peptide fractions showed quite different profiles. The five common N-glycosylated peptides identified in all venoms belong to abundant toxins (SVMP and SVSP), while low-abundant components (5'-Nase and HYA) (Figure  A) also showed a few conserved glycosylated sequences. On the other hand, the 50 conserved peptides identified in the nonglycosylated fractions mapped to eight toxin classes (Figure  B). In general, MS-driven data of snake venom proteomes are analyzed in terms of the comparison of unique and shared toxins, as shown in Figure  B. The comparison of nonglycosylated tryptic peptides shown in Figure  B is an alternative way to evaluate proteome diversity, which, in the case of the venoms analyzed in this study, revealed conserved and variable peptides of various toxin classes and offered a different view of intragenus variability that took into account amino acid sequences and might overcome the bias of comparing venom proteomes rich in proteoforms.

The efficiency of the utilization of N-glycosylation sites depends on the kinetics of the transfer of a lipid-linked oligosaccharide to asparagine residues in sequons of nascent polypeptide chains.   A study on the characterization of the proteome of the venom glands of B. jararaca, taking into account two distinct phases of its ontogenetic development and the marked sexual dimorphism of this species, demonstrated variable abundances of proteins associated with glycosylation processes and folding, in comparisons of newborn x adult and female x male venoms, suggesting that the variation in the expression levels of cellular proteins might give rise to an even higher variation in the expressed toxins. Although no mechanism to determine or impact N-glycosylation site occupancy in snake venom proteins has been demonstrated, the low number of common N-glycosylated peptides identified here suggests that the variability in glycosylation is an important feature of proteomes.

One of the most significant findings of this study was the confirmation of the high sialylation levels of toxins in Bothrops venoms, and the presence of this monosaccharide could be related to a higher half-life time in the prey body. However, sialylation could be important to the toxin function as well, as suggested by studies that explored the importance of sialylated glycan structures in the biological activities of LAAO, SVMP, and SVSP. -   In the case of an LAAO of Calloselasma rhodostoma venom, the N-glycosylation was not necessary for its catalytic activity but was essential for induction of apoptosis. The activities of the sialylated and nonsialylated forms of the SVMP bilitoxin-1 were evaluated by Nikai et al., who showed that sialic acid was not important for substrate hydrolysis, but its removal promoted a decrease of hemorrhagic activity. In the SVSP acutobin, the presence of a sialic acid dimer structure showed to be important for enzymatic activity and protein stability. Furthermore, in a comprehensive study, carbohydrate chains containing sialic acid were shown to play a role in the activity of proteinases of Bothrops venoms upon macromolecular substrates. Besides the importance of N-glycans containing sialic acid in the enzymatic activity of toxins, there is also the possibility of sialylated glycan chains to interact with proteins of the Siglec family (sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-type lectins). These lectins are widely expressed by immune cells, and their engagement by sialylated toxins could play a role in the envenomation process. The occurrence of sialic acid dimers in snake toxins was first identified by Lin et al. and, in our study, it was more often found in toxins of B. alcatraz, B. cotiara, B. fonsecai, B. insularis, and B. jararaca venoms.

In general, the SVMP class showed an average ratio of N-glycosylation heterogeneity below that of the whole venoms (Figure  and Table S26). An N-glycosylation site located in the C-terminal portion of the prodomain and in the vicinity of the catalytic domain was identified in the N-terminomic analysis of B. alcatraz  and B. jararaca venoms as unoccupied. In this study, we identified the same peptide backbone in the venoms of B. alcatraz, B. jararaca, B. jararacussu, and B. moojeni with its N-glycosylation site free and occupied (Tables S18-24 and S27-33). Farther, all N-glycosylated peptides located in the same region of SVMP precursors contained hybrid/complex N-glycans, many of them with sialic acid units, suggesting that the occupation of these N-glycosylation sites conveys a variability source and might affect the structure or activity of the nascent SVMPs (Figure  A). As with other proteinases in which glycosylation sites are located in the pro-domain or in its vicinity, -     we hypothesize that the N-glycosylation site identified in the prodomain of SVMPs could be involved in the control of zymogen activation, and the variable occupancy of this site contributes to the N-terminal variability of the mature forms of this toxin class. In most venoms, the Cys-rich domain showed the highest level of glycosylation heterogeneity (Figures   and A). This domain of the SVMPs has been shown to play a role in their functional activities, serving as an interaction interface with substrates, and directing the toxin to specific sites. -   Thus, besides the hypervariable region of the Cys-rich domain, which is a variable spot in the structure of different SVMPs, N-glycosylation appears to be another feature contributing to variability as the occupation of the sites identified here was variable among the venoms (Figure  A).

Regarding the SVSPs, it is known that glycosylation is an important variability factor, as these proteins may contain distinct numbers of putative N-glycosylation sites. As an example of the significance of glycosylation for some SVSPs of Bothrops venoms, it was shown that the glycan moiety of the heavily glycosylated Bothrops Protease A (BPA) is important for its substrate specificity. In another example, the SVSP PA-BJ, present in B. jararaca venom in at least eight proteoforms, contains an N-glycosylation site close to the catalytic cleft that was proposed not to affect substrate specificity but could avoid the interaction with serpins present in the blood. In agreement with the high variability of occupation of glycosylation sites by N-glycans containing sialic acid in Bothrops venoms (Figure  B), several SVSP preparations showed distinct forms in electrophoresis, with slightly different molecular masses and pIs, due to variations in their amino acid sequences and glycosylation levels. While SVSPs show the same primary specificity as trypsin (Arg or Lys at the P1 position), they exhibit stringent macromolecular substrate specificity in contrast to trypsin, which is putatively not N-glycosylated and lacks specificity upon macromolecular substrates. Hence, the variable positions of putative N-glycosylation sites and their occupation in Bothrops SVSPs are likely a crucial factor conveying functional specificity to these enzymes.

The LAAOs contain variations in their tertiary structures and may show distinct physicochemical properties.   Of special note is the high variability ratio of occupation of a conserved N-glycosylation site identified in LAAOs of the different Bothrops venoms. Even in venoms sharing the same venom N-glycome repertoire, such as B. alcatraz, B. insularis, and B. jararaca, the present study revealed that the occupation of an N-glycosylation site in LAAOs was heterogeneous, representing a variability spot in these toxins (Figures   and C). The carbohydrate moiety of LAAOs has been associated with the ability of the enzymes to interact with the cell surface and enhance the localization of high concentrations of H2O2; thus, the variable occupancy of N-glycosylation sites might be a factor in the modulation of their pathological activities as toxins in the context of the distinct venom proteomes.

As we previously reported,   the analysis of lectin-enriched fractions of venom glycosylated proteins favors the identification of minor components, such as APase, 5'-Nase, and PDE. Even though their role in the envenomation process is poorly understood, the identification of N-glycosylation sites showed that the structural complexity of the venoms involves most components, with the exception of PLA2 and CTL. Overall, while it is not possible to predict or accurately measure the impact of the N-glycosylation process for the structure and function of toxins, future studies on snake venom N-glycosylated toxins should consider the occurrence of this PTM when comparing toxins of the same class.
Conclusions

The application of advanced approaches of mass spectrometry is fundamental for assessing PTMs in proteins of nonmodel organisms, such as snakes. This study represents the first report on the deep, high-throughput identification of snake venom N-glycoproteomes. The integrated application of MS-driven analysis of N-glycan chains and peptide backbones allowed the identification of N-glycosylated sites in venom proteins and their roles in intraspecies venom complexity and variability. This study also confirmed that N-glycan compositions belonging to the hybrid/complex class are a variability source, mainly in phylogenetically distant species. Moreover, it showed that, except for PLA2, all other venom enzymes are N-glycosylated, and, in general, sialylation and fucosylation are prominent features of N-glycans in all analyzed venoms.

Considering that the venom samples used in this study were composed of variable amounts of individual venoms, it is possible that individual variability may have contributed to an unpredictable additive effect on the compositions of glycoproteomes. Hence, ideally, an accurate comparison of these species would embody the knowledge of individual venoms. Furthermore, the extensive identification of N-glycopeptides reported here does not allow for the determination of the stoichiometry of all protein glycoforms in the venoms. Nevertheless, the results of this study confirmed the widely accepted notion that viperid snake venoms show a variety of modified and nonmodified toxin proteoforms.

It is not possible to unveil the function of glycosylation in a toxin without specific studies to assess the relationships between the structure and biological activity, and there is no general role that could be attributed to it. However, factors like the energy cost of venom production -   and the conservation of the presence of N-glycosylated toxins during the evolution process indicate that N-glycosylation is an important feature of the venom proteome phenotype.

Feeding habits have been associated with the variability of snake venom composition, and microheterogeneities of toxins, such as N-glycosylation, can be seen as functional signatures of the variability in snake venoms that could be involved in the ability of different species to deal with different types of prey. The fine-tuning mechanism of occupation of N-glycosylation sites can be considered as (1) parsimonious, since changes in glycan composition or in the occupation of the sequons contribute to the generation of different glycoforms, and (2) functional, since structural changes could lead to new targets in different types of prey. Nevertheless, the diversity of glycoproteins in venoms of the Viperidae family is impressive; hence, it is possible that the use of N-sequons and the assembly of N-glycan chains are basic strategies of structural diversification of toxins and not influenced by diet.

The knowledge about the location and occupation of N-glycosylation sites in snake venoms should help in the exploration of the role N-glycans could play in the function of each toxin. Further, with the recent possibility of cultivating functional organoids derived from snake venom glands, researchers have more tools to generate toxins directly from this system and create new ways to study the role of N-glycosylation on specific toxin sites without the bias of the heterologous production of recombinant proteins.

Therefore, paradoxically, Bothrops venom phenotypes are conserved and divergent, indicating that evolution and divergence in the venom composition among species might be related to evolutionary responses to diet, habitat, and predator-prey interactions, and need further studies to be fully understood.

Typically, variation in venom toxins is attributed to gene duplication and the effect of positive selection, leading to the production of functionally distinct venoms and possibly affecting the effectiveness of antivenom treatments. Our results clearly show that variable protein glycosylation is another molecular mechanism that contributes to variability and should be taken into account when investigating venom functional evolution.

Whether the variability that originated from the N-glycan structures is a coordinated action of glycosidases and glycosyltransferases of functional significance for the mature glycoprotein in the venom or merely an expected, stochastic generation of biologically neutral diversity is a relevant question that needs further studies to build on evidence to achieve a solid response.

The contradictory aspects of conservation of the venom phenotype framework and diversification of glycan usage, in parallel to Bothrops species clustering according to phylogeny, offer the opportunity for further studies to gain insights into the determinants of toxin structure and function evolution.

passages.text: Schiff Base Compound of (E)-1-(((4-chloro-2-hydroxyphenyl)imino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol as CDK2 Inhibitory Agent: Structural Characterization, Density Functional Theory Computational, and In Silico studies
ABSTRACT

Compound (E)-1-(((4-chloro-2-hydroxyphenyl)imino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol (HNC) was prepared by the reaction between 2-hydroxynaphthyl-1-carboxaldehyde and 2-amino-5-chlorophenol in an equimolar ratio and obtained in moderate yield. HNC was characterized using physicochemical and various spectroscopic techniques. The slow evaporation of a hot methanolic solution of HNC resulted in the formation of the zwitterionic ketoenamine form of HNC, and denoted as HNC'. Structurally, HNC' comprises one naphthoxide ring bridged with one chlorophenol ring by the azomethine group, and the torsion angle between the naphthoxide and the chlorophenol ring is 11.78 , speculating a nonplanar geometry. The density functional theory (DFT) at M06-2X/def2-TZVP level of theory described the facile enolimine-ketoenamine tautomerism and the highest occupied molecular orbital-lowest unoccupied molecular orbital gap of 5.757 eV for HNC, consistent with a moderately reactive scaffold. The inhibitory potential of HNC against cyclin-dependent kinases 2 (CDK2) was evaluated using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and molecular mechanics generalized Born surface area (MM-GBSA) free energy calculations. Docking results showed that HNC achieved a binding score of -8.75 kcal/mol, slightly lower than the reference inhibitor Roscovitine (RVT), which scored -9.41 kcal/mol. MM-GBSA calculations yielded DeltaGtotal values of -40.95 kcal/mol for HNC and -41.14 kcal/mol for RVT, suggesting comparable binding affinities. Generally, our findings pose HNC as a credible CDK2 inhibitor and tractable starting point for optimization toward selective antiproliferative agents.
Introduction

Cancer remains one of the top causes of mortality globally, and every year, millions of new cases and cancer-related fatalities are recorded worldwide. In 2022, approximately 9.7 million people died as a result of cancer, and 20 million new cases were reported according to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (affiliated with the World Health Organization). This report was alarming; thus, cancer can be seen as a prominent global health concern. Cancer develops when cells proliferate abnormally, resulting in malignant tumors that negatively impact surrounding tissues as well as other vital body organs. Significant progress has been made in combating cancer disease, and this includes early diagnosis in conjunction with various modalities like radiation, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy. However, the multifaceted nature of cancer cells and their capacity to develop adaptive resistance still hinder clinical results and result in poor prognosis. This highlights the pressing need for novel therapeutic approaches that minimize off-target damage while specifically disrupting cancer cells. One of the key strategies adopted in anticancer drug development is targeting signal pathways that regulate rapid cell division and growth of tumor cells. One of the enzymes that controls these pathways is cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs). Thus, targeting CDKs disrupts the signal pathway, resulting in the suppression of excessive cell growth, thereby leading to the cure of cancer.

CDKs are enzymes that play crucial roles in DNA repair, regulation of the eukaryotic cell cycle, transcription, together with display critical functions in cellular apoptosis and differentiation. Of the many CDKs, CDK2 is essential for controlling the cell cycle, and its overexpression has been associated with unusual cell cycle control, which results in hyperproliferation of cancer cells. Since abnormal CDK2 expression is linked to several cancer types, such as ovarian cancer, CDK2 has been thoroughly investigated and proven to be an effective target for cancer treatment. Several compounds, which include Dinaciclib, olomucine, Roscovitine (RVT), and flavopiridol, have shown promising potential to inhibit CDK2. However, during clinical studies on the treatment of cancer disease, that is, breast cancer, they were reported to be ineffective due to their non-specific pan-CDK cytotoxicity and several side effects. Hence, there is a need to develop novel CDK2 inhibitors with great potential to be used as anticancer drugs with no or fewer adverse effects.

passages.text: The use of relevant computational software in the discovery of drugs has gained prominence in the past decades. Dating back to the 1980s, the computer-aided approach has facilitated the process of drug discovery and helped to lower the cost incurred by conventional ways of developing drugs. Drug design and development using computational techniques is based on several fundamental principles, including drug-target interaction and binding, and these can be achieved using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation, among other available computational approaches. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) has been identified as one of the unique and effective computational techniques used in probing electronic properties and the stability of molecules. It also helps in simulating the geometry of molecules, most especially in the absence of single X-ray crystal structures.

In this study, we explore molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation studies to probe the inhibitory potential of (E)-1-(((4-chloro-2-hydroxyphenyl)imino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol (HNC) against CDK2. Furthermore, we use DFT studies to gain insight into the tautomerism existing between the enolimine form of HNC and the ketoenamine form (HNC') and also utilize it to investigate the electronic and chemical reactivity properties of HNC. Our motivation stems from the preliminary results obtained from SwissTargetPrediction while searching for potential biomolecular targets for HNC, and the outcome predicted CDK2 as a possible target with high probability. Compound HNC belongs to a group of organic compounds named Schiff bases, and they are usually prepared by the condensation reaction between primary amines and carbonyl compounds (aldehydes or ketones) under suitable reaction conditions. Sekar et al. reported the inhibitory potential of (Z)-2-((4,6-diphenyl-5,6-dihydro-4H-1,3-thiazin-2-yl)imino)-2,3-dihydro-1H-inden-1-one (a Chalcone-Schiff base hybrid) against CDK2, which showed superior activities over the reference drugs used for the study. Compound HNC comprises substituents such as hydroxyl, chlorine, and the naphthalene ring. These substituents have been reported to play a crucial role in the potency of medicinal drugs. For example, hydroxyl functional groups of Schiff bases increase hydrogen bonding with protein residues of biomolecular targets and improve their inhibitory potential. Furthermore, the availability of a chlorine atom in HNC would also improve its lipophilicity and promote hydrophobic interactions, which are relevant for occupying the ATP-binding pocket of kinases such as CDK2. The extended conjugated pi-system presence in HNC due to the naphthalene ring might also favor pi-pi stacking interactions with aromatic residues in the active site of CDK2. We projected that these substituents in the structural backbone of HNC make it a good drug candidate for CDK2. Here, we report the synthesis and inhibitory potential of HNC against CDK2.
Reagents, Instrumentation, and Experimental Procedures
Solvents and Reagents

The core reagents utilized in the synthesis of HNC are 2-amino-5-chlorophenol (97%), 2-hydroxynaphthyl-1-carboxaldehyde (98%), and acetic acid (>=99.7%), while the solvents used are methanol (>=99.8%), hexane (>=99%), and diethyl ether (>=99%). They are all ACS grades, used without further purification and obtained from Merck.
Instrumentation

The 1H as well as 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra of HNC were obtained in d-DMSO by exploring a Bruker AvanceIII 600 MHz spectrometer at 25 C. The peaks due to residual d-DMSO were observed at 2.50 ppm and delta 39.52 ppm in 1H and 13C NMR spectra, respectively. The Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectrum was determined by a Nicolet Avatar 330 FT-IR spectrometer coupled with ZnSe 1455 ATR. The elemental/CHN analysis was recorded using the Vario elemental E.L. cube CHNS analyzer. The mass spectrum of HNC was obtained using a Waters SYNAPT G2 coupled to a Waters Ultra-performance Liquid Chromatography, electrospray ionization (ESI) probe, ESI Positive, Cone Voltage 15 V, while for the melting point, an SMP20 melting point instrument was used. A GBC UV/Vis 920 spectrophotometer was used to record the UV-visible spectrum of HNC.
Synthesis of HNC

The compound HNC was synthesized by the condensation reaction between 2-hydroxynaphthyl-1-carboxaldehyde and 2-amino-5-chlorophenol in an equimolar ratio following the procedure reported in the literature with slight modifications. In summary, 2.323 mmol of methanolic (20 mL of methanol) solution of 2-hydroxynaphthyl-1-carboxaldehyde solution was added to 2.323 mmol of methanolic (20 mL of methanol) solution of 2-amino-5-chlorophenol in a 100 mL round-bottom flask, and 4 -5 drops of acetic acid were added to the resulting solution. The resultant mixture was stirred vigorously for 2 h at room temperature, and an orange precipitate of HNC crashed out of the solution. The crude HNC was thoroughly rinsed with diethyl ether to remove unreacted amine and then dried in an oven at 50 C overnight.
Synthesis of HNC
Single-Crystal X-ray Crystallography

The crystal structure of the ketoenamine form of HNC was obtained instead of the imine form and denoted as HNC'. The appropriate crystal of HNC' used for this experiment was obtained by gradual evaporation of a hot (70-80 C) methanolic solution of HNC for approximately 3 days. A crystal of HNC' with dimensions 0.198 x 0.093 x 0.032 mm3 was mounted on a Bruker APEX II DUO CCD diffractometer with radiation (0.71073 A) at a temperature of 100 K. The structure of HNC' was solved and refined by exploring SHELXT within the X-Seed environment. The refined parameters together with structural data are presented in Table 1, while molecular graphics are obtained by Mercury software.

Computational Methodology
DFT Studies

All quantum chemical calculations in this study were carried out using DFT as implemented in the Gaussian 16 software package. The molecular geometries were fully optimized without symmetry constraints using the M06-2X functional, a hybrid meta-GGA functional known for its accuracy in describing non-covalent interactions and thermochemical properties. The def2-TZVP basis set was employed for all atoms, offering a good balance between computational cost and accuracy due to its triple-zeta quality and polarization functions. Vibrational frequency analysis was carried out to confirm the nature of each optimized structure. The structure identified as a transition state was validated by the presence of a single imaginary frequency in its vibrational mode. Furthermore, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) calculations were performed to ensure that the transition state properly connects the intended reactant and product along the reaction pathway. To account for solution effects, single-point energy (SPE) calculations were performed on the gas-phase optimized structures at the same level of theory. These calculations employed the SMD solvation model with methanol as the solvent. Unless otherwise stated, the Gibbs free energies in solution were used for discussion, and they were evaluated at 298.15 K and 1 atm. For illustrative purposes, selected key intermediates and transition states were visualized using the CLYview software.

Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) energies, including the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) levels, were calculated to evaluate the molecule's electronic properties and energy gap (DeltaE). Key global reactivity descriptors such as ionization potential (IP), electron affinity (EA), chemical hardness (eta), softness (sigma), electronegativity (chi), and electrophilicity index (omega) were derived from these orbital energies. To investigate the nature of intramolecular interactions and electron delocalization, natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis was conducted using the NBO 7.0 module embedded within Gaussian. This allowed identification of donor-acceptor interactions and second-order perturbation energies (E(2)) for assessing conjugative effects. The molecular electrostatic potential (MESP) maps were generated to visualize charge distribution across the molecular surface and identify regions susceptible to electrophilic or nucleophilic attack. Additionally, Mulliken atomic charge analysis was performed to interpret electronic polarization effects further. All molecular visualizations, including HOMO-LUMO plots, MESP surfaces, and NBO interaction diagrams, were rendered using GaussView 6.0 and OriginLab, ensuring accurate interpretation and presentation of electronic structure features.
Molecular Docking Studies
Ligands and Protein Preparation

The 2D structure of HNC was converted to 3D and prepared using LigPrep (Schrodinger, Release 2023-2), applying the OPLS4 force field, generating possible ionization states at pH 7.0 +- 2.0. The crystal structure of CDK2 was retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB ID: 2A4L) and processed using the Protein Preparation Wizard. Missing side chains and hydrogens were added, bond orders were assigned, and protonation states were optimized. Water molecules beyond 3 A from heteroatoms were deleted.
Molecular Docking

Prepared ligands were docked into the CDK2 active site using Glide XP (Extra Precision) mode. A grid box centered on the co-crystallized ligand was generated. Docking scores were evaluated, and docking pose validation was confirmed by re-docking the native ligand with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.31 A.
Molecular Dynamics Simulations

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were conducted using AMBER20. The ff14SB force field was applied to the protein, and ligand parameters were generated using Antechamber with the GAFF2 force field. The system was solvated in a TIP3P water box with 10 A of any box edge, neutralized with counter ions, minimized, equilibrated, and run for 120 ns under NPT conditions at 300 K and 1 atm. Post-simulation analysis, including RMSD, root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), and radius of gyration (RoG), was done using CPPTRAJ and plotted using Origin 6.0. Binding affinities were estimated using molecular mechanics generalized Born surface area (MM-GBSA) via the MMPBSA.py script on 1000 snapshots extracted from the last 120 ns of the MD trajectory. The total binding free energy (DeltaG_total) and its components (van der Waals, electrostatics, and solvation) were computed for each complex.
Results and Discussion
Synthesis of HNC

The synthetic pathway for the preparation of HNC is shown in Scheme 1. This was achieved by the condensation reaction between 2-hydroxynaphthyl-1-carboxaldehyde and 2-amino-5-chlorophenol in a 1:1 ratio. Compound HNC was obtained as an air-stable orange solid in a good yield of about 68% and displayed a melting point within the range of 268-270 C. HNC readily dissolves in DMSO and partially dissolves in methanol and ethanol. However, at high temperature, around 70-80 C, it dissolves completely in methanol and ethanol. Furthermore, HNC is insoluble in chloroform, dichloromethane, hexane, and toluene.
Synthesis of HNC.
Spectroscopy Elucidation
1H and 13C NMR

The 1H-NMR spectrum for HNC was obtained using deuterated DMSO as solvent and is presented in Figure S1. The diagnostic peaks, i.e., the peaks for hydroxyl, aromatic, and azomethine protons, are all observed in the spectrum. In the downfield region, two peaks are observed as a singlet at 10.83 ppm and 15.70 ppm, respectively, and these can be assigned to the protons due to nap-OH and Ar-OH, respectively. The proton attached to the naphthalene ring (nap-OH) appeared at a higher chemical shift when compared to the one attached to the phenyl ring (Ar-OH) due to its participation in hydrogen bonding with the nitrogen atom of the azomethine functional group (CH N). The azomethine proton (CH N) appeared as a singlet at 9.52 ppm, and this value is similar to those previously reported for related compounds. The aromatic protons for both the naphthalene and benzene ring appeared as either a doublet or triplet within the range of 6.83-8.41 ppm, Figure S1. In the 13C-NMR spectrum, the peaks for the aromatic carbons appeared around 108.52-176.81 ppm, Figure S2. The naphthalene and benzene carbons directly attached to the hydroxyl group appeared at 176.81 and 150.14 ppm. They appeared at a higher chemical shift when compared to other aromatic carbons due to the deshielding effect of the hydroxyl group. The azomethine carbon appeared at 150.87 ppm.
FT-IR, Mass, and Electronic Absorption Spectra

In the FT-IR spectrum of HNC, two major diagnostic vibrational bands were observed. These are vibrational bands due to v(C:Hstr) and v(C Nstr), and they appeared around 3100-2900 and 1616 cm-1, respectively, Figure S3. The vibrational band due to v(C Cstr) of naphthalene and benzene rings was observed within 1543-1586 cm-1, while the one due to v(C:Ostr) was observed around 1209 cm-1. It is very difficult to observe the vibrational band due to v(O:Hstr) in the FT-IR spectrum of HNC, and this might be due to its involvement in hydrogen bonding.

The mass spectrum of HNC reveals its [M+H]+ and [M+H+2]+ peaks at 298.0631 and 300.0611, respectively. The intensity of the [M]+ and [M+2]+ is 3:1, and this affirms the presence of one chlorine atom in HNC. Figure 1 depicts the electronic absorption spectrum of HNC, which was obtained using its dimethyl sulfoxide solution within the range of 200 - 800 nm. Two major bands were observed. The first band was observed around 328-329 nm, and this can be assigned to n pi* due to the azomethine (C N) functional group. The second band appeared split within the range of 451-474 nm in the visible region, and this can be assigned to pi pi* of the extended conjugated system of the aromatic moiety in the compound. The splitting of the band might be a result of DMSO interacting with the HNC (solvent-solute interactions).
Ultraviolet (UV)-visible spectrum of HNC.
Single-Crystal X-ray Crystallography Analysis of HNC

The slow evaporation of a hot methanolic solution of HNC (enolimine form) affords the ketoenamine form of HNC, which is denoted as HNC'. The conversion of HNC to HNC' occurs at a temperature around 70-80 C and leads to the complete transfer of a hydrogen atom from the naphtholic group to the azomethine nitrogen, Figure S5. This phenomenon is known as tautomerism, and it results in the :OH tautomer (enolimine form) and :C O tautomer (ketoenamine form). Figure 2 shows the molecular structure of HNC', and selected bond distances together with bond angles are given in Table 2. Compound HNC' crystallizes as orthorhombic with a space group of Pbca and has a whole molecule in its asymmetric structure. Compound HNC' has 8 asymmetric structures in its unit cell as revealed by its packing diagram, Figure S6. HNC' comprises one naphthoxide ring bridged with one chlorophenol ring by an azomethine functional group. The naphthoxide ring is almost coplanar with the azomethine moiety (CH N) as revealed by their torsion angle of 179.9(4)  for C17:C8:C7:N1, while the phenol ring deviates from the azomethine moiety plane as seen from the torsion angle of C7:N1:C4:C3 to be 170.8(4)  (Table 2). The torsion angle between the naphthoxide and the phenol ring is 11.78 , suggesting a nonplanar geometry. The values for C7:N1 and C9:O2 are 1.311 A and 1.293 A, respectively, and this depicts that C7:N1 is longer than the C N bond while C9:O2 is shorter than C:O. This feature reflects the zwitterionic nature of HNC'. It was also observed that HNC' was stabilized via intramolecular N:H   O Cnaph hydrogen bonding with a bond strength of 1.858 A. Moreso, there is an intermolecular hydrogen bond via O:H   O Cnaph with a bond strength of 1.682 A, forming a 1D supramolecular structure which extends along the crystallographic b plane (Figure 3).

DFT Studies
Geometry Optimization

The geometry of HNC was optimized using DFT calculations. In this geometry, the molecule features an imino functional group (-CH N-), substituted at the imino carbon and nitrogen atoms by phenolic rings, respectively. Specifically, the imino carbon is connected to a 2-naphthol moiety, while the imino nitrogen is substituted with a 5-chlorophenol group. The optimized structure reveals an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the iminic nitrogen (N19) and the hydroxyl hydrogen (H21) of the 2-naphthol fragment, with a hydrogen bond distance of 1.64 A. This interaction contributes to the overall structural stability of HNC. The tautomerization of HNC to its ketoenamine counterpart, denoted HNC', was further investigated. This tautomerization involves a proton transfer from the hydroxyl group of the 2-naphthol moiety (O17-H21) to the imine nitrogen, via a transition state, TS1. The favorable orientation of the hydroxyl proton (H21) toward the imine nitrogen facilitates this intramolecular proton transfer. The calculated Gibbs free energy barrier for this process is almost barrierless (0.60 kcal/mol). The resulting ketoenamine intermediate (HNC') is thermodynamically more stable than HNC by only 0.50 kcal/mol, suggesting the possibility of the two isomers interconverting to one another.

Two intramolecular hydrogen bonds further stabilize HNC'. The first occurs between the transferred proton (H21) and the deprotonated naphthanolic oxygen (O17), with a hydrogen bond distance of 1.79 A (O17 H21). The second hydrogen bond interaction is between the same hydrogen (H21) and the hydroxyl oxygen of the chlorophenol fragment (O31), with a bond distance of 2.22 A (O31 H21). Although the overall energy difference between HNC and HNC' is minimal (0.50 kcal/mol in favor of HNC'), it aligns with the experimentally observed thermodynamic preference for the ketoenamine form. It supports the possibility of facile interconversion between the two tautomers (Figure 4).
Energy profile of the enolimine-ketoenamine tautomerism of HNC with their relative energies in kcal/mol. Bond distances are in A.
Quantum Chemical Descriptors

Compound HNC crystallizes in the ketoenamine form rather than the enolimine form, and in order to gain insight into the electronic, chemical reactivity, and stability of HNC, we explored computational techniques to unravel these properties. The FMO analysis serves as a fundamental tool to understand the electronic behavior and chemical reactivity of the HNC molecule. As illustrated in the upper part of Figure 5, the HOMO and LUMO are spatially distributed over the conjugated pi-system of the molecule, with particular contributions from electronegative atoms like nitrogen and oxygen. The HOMO represents the molecule's ability to donate electrons, whereas the LUMO signifies its electron-accepting capability. The computed energy levels of the HOMO and LUMO are -6.985 eV and -1.228 eV, respectively, yielding an energy gap (DeltaE) of 5.757 eV. This relatively large band gap indicates a molecule that is electronically stable and less prone to spontaneous electronic excitation. Such a gap also implies that the molecule requires a moderate amount of energy to transition from the ground to the excited state, making it suitable for optoelectronic and sensing applications.
Highest occupied molecular orbital-lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (HOMO-LUMO) and molecular electrostatic potential (MESP) plots for HNC.

Additionally, from these orbital energies, several reactivity descriptors are derived. The IP and EA are obtained directly from the HOMO and LUMO energies, with values of 1.228 and 6.985 eV, respectively (Table 3). These indicate that the molecule is more receptive to gaining electrons than losing them, further supporting its electrophilic character. The chemical hardness (eta), calculated as 2.879 eV, suggests that the molecule resists deformation of its electron cloud, while the chemical softness (sigma), the reciprocal of eta, is 0.174 eV-1. Together, these parameters show that the HNC molecule is chemically stable but possesses moderate reactivity, primarily due to its electrophilic nature. The orbital topologies and energy gap align well with the calculated electrophilicity index (omega = 2.93 eV). This strengthens the conclusion that the molecule can act as a strong electron acceptor in intermolecular interactions. Compound HNC exhibits a net dipole moment of 2.42 Debye.

Molecular Electrostatic Potential

The MESP surface, shown in the lower panel of Figure 5, provides a perceptive visualization of the electronic distribution across the HNC molecule, particularly in terms of regions susceptible to electrophilic or nucleophilic attack. In this surface representation, regions colored blue to green indicate electron-rich zones (nucleophilic centers), while red to yellow denote electron-deficient zones (electrophilic centers). The non-uniformity observed across the molecule reflects the heteroatomic contributions (notably nitrogen, oxygen, and halogens), which influence the molecule's reactivity landscape. This MESP map aligns well with the computed electrophilicity index (omega) of 2.93 eV derived from FMO analysis, as tabulated in the quantum chemical descriptors. A moderate-to-high omega value suggests that the molecule has a significant tendency to accept electrons, confirming its electrophilic nature. This is further supported by the chemical potential (mu = -4.107 eV) and chemical hardness (eta = 2.879 eV), indicating a relatively stable but reactive system. Thus, the integration of MESP visualization with FMO-derived descriptors such as the electrophilicity index provides a comprehensive understanding of the molecule's reactive tendencies. It validates the conclusion that the HNC molecule is well-suited for interactions involving electron-rich species.
Natural Bond Orbital

The NBO analysis offers critical insights into the electronic delocalization and intramolecular interactions that govern the stability and reactivity of compound HNC. By identifying donor-acceptor interactions between filled (donor) and empty (acceptor) orbitals, the NBO approach helps quantify electron density transfer within the molecule, providing a deeper understanding of its bonding characteristics. In the case of HNC, several significant interactions were identified, with stabilization energies (E(2)) indicating the extent of delocalization. The most prominent interaction is the pi   pi* donation from the C24-C27 bond to the C21-C22 antibonding orbital, with an exceptionally high E(2) value of 316.39 kcal/mol and a minimal energy gap (DeltaE = 0.01 a.u), suggesting a highly efficient electron delocalization along this conjugated segment. This extensive delocalization plays a crucial role in stabilizing the molecular framework and reinforcing pi-conjugation throughout the aromatic system. Another strong interaction is observed between pi(C11-C14) and pi* (C10-C15), which contributes 138.74 kcal/mol in stabilization energy (Table  4 ). This indicates strong resonance interaction across adjacent aromatic rings. The presence of lone pair (LP) donation, such as LP(1) on C3   pi*(C1-C2) with 64.27 kcal/mol, further highlights the role of nonbonding electron density in stabilizing the conjugated pi-system and creating localized regions of electron richness. Less intense, yet still noteworthy, pi   pi* interactions include C23-C26 to C24-C27 (32.03 kcal/mol) and C21-C22 to C23-C26 (29.03 kcal/mol). These interactions collectively depict a highly interconnected electronic system, suggesting that electrons are extensively delocalized across multiple bonds, which enhances the molecule's electronic communication and structural integrity.

Such delocalization not only imparts additional thermodynamic stability but also influences the molecule's reactivity, making it more capable of participating in charge-transfer processes. The Mulliken charge distribution, as illustrated in Figure 6a,b, offers an understanding of the electron density distribution within HNC. Molecular Docking and MD Simulation Studies
Molecular Docking

The molecular docking studies of HNC against CDK2 were conducted using Schrodinger software to evaluate its potential as an inhibitory agent. The docking score for HNC was determined to be -8.75 kcal/mol, reflecting a favorable binding affinity to the CDK2 active site. In comparison, the reference drug RVT, a well-established CDK2 inhibitor, achieved a docking score of -9.41 kcal/mol, indicating a slightly higher affinity. These results provide initial evidence supporting the potential of the compound as a CDK2 inhibitor despite its marginally lower binding strength relative to RVT.

A superimposed structure analysis was performed to validate the docking protocol. Figure 7a presents the superimposed structures of RVT and HNC within the same binding pocket, offering a comparative view of their binding orientations. Figure 7b displays the superimposed structures of the native ligand RVT and its redocked counterpart, with an RMSD of 1.31 A, which confirms the reliability of the docking methodology. The close alignment between the native and redocked RVT structures ensures that the predicted binding poses and interactions for HNC are consistent with the established crystallographic data of CDK2, laying a robust foundation for further exploration.

(a) Superimposed structures of Roscovitine (RVT) and HNC within the CDK2 binding pocket. (b) Superimposed structures of the native ligand RVT and its redocked counterpart, with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 1.31 A.

However, despite these promising docking results, the methodology has inherent limitations. Docking scores, while helpful in assessing binding potential, do not fully capture the dynamic nature of protein-ligand interactions or the entropic contributions to binding stability, both of which are critical for determining an inhibitor's efficacy in a physiological context. This suggests that the slightly lower docking score for HNC (-8.75 kcal/mol) compared to RVT (-9.41 kcal/mol) may not fully reflect its true inhibitory potential. As noted in previous studies addressing similar computational challenges, the static nature of docking limits its ability to account for long-term stability and conformational adaptability. To address these limitations, subsequent molecular dynamics simulations are essential to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of HNC's interactions and stability within the CDK2 active site.
Protein-Ligand Interactions Analysis

The protein-ligand interaction profiles for HNC and RVT with CDK2 are shown in Figure 8a,b, to complement the docking scores. Compound HNC (Figure 8a), with a docking score of -8.75 kcal/mol, forms conventional hydrogen bonds with LYS33 and ASP145, and pi-alkyl interactions with ALA144, LEU134, ILE10, VAL18, and ALA31, indicating a mix of polar and hydrophobic engagements. Van der Waals interactions with ASP86, GLU12, LEU83, and other residues stabilize the complex. RVT (Figure 8b), with a docking score of -9.41 kcal/mol, exhibits conventional hydrogen bonds with GLU12 and LEU83, a carbon-hydrogen bond with PHE82, a pi-cation interaction with LYS89, a pi-sigma interaction with PHE80, and pi-alkyl interactions with VAL64, ALA31, LEU134, and others, alongside van der Waals contacts. The broader interaction profile of RVT, including the unique pi-cation bond, likely contributes to its higher affinity. Both ligands share similar binding poses, but HNC's slightly lower score suggests the need for molecular dynamics simulations to assess dynamic stability, given docking's static limitations. Table 5 provides a summarized view of the key docking interactions for HNC and RVT, emphasizing hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts as derived from Figure 8.

MD Simulation

MD simulations were performed using Amber20 to evaluate the stability and dynamics of CDK2 in its complex with HNC, RVT, and the apoprotein (APO) over a 120 ns trajectory. Post-MD analysis was conducted using CPPTRAJ to compute key parameters, each serving a specific purpose. The RMSD assesses the overall structural stability and deviation of the protein-ligand complex from its initial conformation over time. The RMSF measures the flexibility and local mobility of individual residues, providing insights into regions of the protein that may be affected by ligand binding. The RoG evaluates the compactness and global conformational changes of the protein structure during the simulation.

The RMSD analysis (Figure 9a) revealed average values of 1.75 A for APO, 1.66 A for APO+RVT, and 1.75 A for APO+HNC, indicating stable complexes with minimal deviation, though APO and APO+HNC exhibited slightly higher fluctuations. RMSF analysis (Figure 9b) showed average values of 0.93 A for APO, 0.87 A for APO+RVT, and 0.87 A for APO+HNC, suggesting comparable residue flexibility, with ligand-bound systems displaying reduced fluctuations. RoG analysis (Figure 9C) yielded averages of 19.78 A for APO, 19.74 A for APO+RVT, and 19.74 A for APO+HNC, reflecting similar compactness across all systems. These results indicate that HNC maintains stability and structural integrity within the CDK2 active site, which is comparable to RVT, supporting its potential as an inhibitor.

(a) Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) plots of CDK2 apoprotein (APO), APO+Roscovitine (RVT), and APO+HNC; (b) root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) plots of APO, APO+RVT, and APO+HNC; (c) radius of gyration (RoG) plots of APO, APO+RVT, and APO+HNC over 120 ns.
Snapshot Analysis of CDK2-HNC Interactions using MD Simulations

The snapshots of HNC with CDK2 at 1 ns, 40 ns, 80 ns, and 120 ns (Figure 10a - 10d) offer a moderate evaluation of its binding stability over the 120 ns molecular dynamics simulation. HNC consistently maintains conventional hydrogen bonds with LYS 33 and ASP 133 across all snapshots, reflecting a stable core interaction. At 1 ns (Figure 10a), an additional carbon-hydrogen bond forms between LYS 112 and the chloride atom, complemented by pi-alkyl interactions around the naphthalene ring with ALA 31, ALA 132, and VAL 52, and van der Waals contacts with GLU 12, GLY 13, and LEU 71. By 40 ns (Figure 10b), pi-alkyl interactions continue with ALA 31, VAL 18, and LEU 122, alongside similar van der Waals contacts. At 80 ns (Figure 10c), pi-alkyl interactions include ALA 31, LEU 122, and VAL 52, with van der Waals contacts involving GLU 12, GLY 13, and ASN 120. At 120 ns (Figure 10d), pi-alkyl interactions persist with ALA 31, LEU 122, and VAL 52, accompanied by van der Waals contacts with GLU 12, GLY 13, and PHE 70, and a pi-pi T-shaped interaction with PHE 68. The sustained hydrogen bonding with LYS 33 and ASP 133, supported by stable pi-alkyl and van der Waals interactions, correlates with RMSD (1.75 A) and RMSF (0.87 A) data, confirming HNC's stability comparable to RVT.
Snapshots of HNC interactions with CDK2 at (a) 1 ns, (b) 40 ns, (c) 80 ns, and (d) 120 ns.
MM-GBSA Bind Free Energy Analysis

The MM-GBSA binding free energy calculations provide a comprehensive evaluation of the binding affinities of HNC and RVT to CDK2, as shown in Table 6. The total binding free energy (DeltaGtotal) for RVT is -41.14 kcal/mol, slightly more favorable than HNC's -40.95 kcal/mol, indicating comparable binding strengths. The gas-phase energy (DeltaGgas) contribution is -69.91 kcal/mol for RVT and -68.66 kcal/mol for HNC, driven primarily by strong van der Waals (vdW) interactions (-51.20 kcal/mol for RVT and -38.99 kcal/mol for HNC) and electrostatic energies (EEL) (-18.71 kcal/mol for RVT and -29.67 kcal/mol for HNC), with HNC showing a more negative EEL due to enhanced polar interactions. The solvation free energy (DeltaGsolv) is positive for both, with values of 28.77 kcal/mol for RVT and 27.71 kcal/mol for HNC, comprising the non-polar surface energy (ESURF) (-6.22 kcal/mol for RVT and -5.34 kcal/mol for HNC) and the polar solvation energy (EGB) (35.00 kcal/mol for RVT and 33.06 kcal/mol for HNC), which partially offsets the favorable DeltaGgas. These MM-GBSA results align with the docking scores (-8.75 kcal/mol for HNC and -9.41 kcal/mol for RVT) and post-MD simulation data, reinforcing HNC's stable and effective binding to CDK2, comparable to RVT.
Binding free energy values for (E)-1-(((4-chloro-2-hydroxyphenyl)imino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol (HNC) and reference Roscovitine (RVT).

Correlation Between Electronic Properties, Reactivity, and Drug-Likeness

The analysis of the FMO of HNC showed that the energy gap between HOMO and LUMO is 5.757 eV, which corresponds to moderate reactivity. Such a stability/reactivity balance is essential to drug-like molecules because it enables them to maintain adequate persistence under physiological environments but still be able to form constructive interactions with the biological targets. The lower HOMO (-1.228 eV) and LUMO (-6.985 eV) energies imply that HNC can act as the electron donor and acceptor, which increases its flexibility in the CDK2 binding pocket. These findings are supported by global reactivity descriptors. The electronegativity (4.107 eV), the chemical potential (-4.107 eV), and the hardness (2.879 eV), as well as the softness (0.174 eV-1), are indicative of the electron-attracting and the balanced reactivity profile, respectively. HNC is located in the moderate electrophile range (omega = 2.930 eV), indicating that it has the potential to establish stabilizing interactions with nucleophilic residues in proteins. This profile is commonly linked to desirable drug-likeness, since it reduces nonspecific reactivity but does not reduce binding.

The analysis of NBO also illustrates that there is a great deal of intramolecular charge delocalization. Its high donor-acceptor interaction reactions, including pi(C24-C27)   pi(C21-C22) (316.39 kcal/mol) and pi(C11-C14)   pi(C10-C15) (138.74 kcal/mol), indicate strong delocalization effects that stabilize the molecule and may contribute to conformational rigidity. Such stabilization is crucial for maintaining bioactive conformations during binding. Lesser but notable interactions, such as LP(1)C3   pi*(C1-C2), also reveal localized charge transfer, enhancing reactivity at specific sites that may interact with polar residues within CDK2.

HNC exhibits extremely comparable binding energetics compared to the reference inhibitor RVT. The free energy calculations using MM-GBSA provided a DeltaGtotal value of -40.95 kcal/mol of HNC and -41.14 kcal/mol of RVT, highlighting their similar affinities. While the interaction profile of RVT is somewhat more diversified, with a pi-cation bond, HNC compensates through strong hydrogen bonding (with LYS33 and ASP133) and van der Waals contacts. Electronic versatility, derived as a result of the HOMO-LUMO and NBO analysis of HNC, is probably the cause of this similar performance, which enables HNC to replicate the ability of the clinically tested inhibitor. Thus, the HOMO-LUMO profile, global reactivity descriptors, and the NBO charge delocalization results all culminate to describe that HNC has an electronic structure compatible with biological activity. Its moderate reactivity, ability to engage in donor-acceptor interactions, and capacity for intramolecular stabilization support its drug-like behavior and rationalize its binding to CDK2 with comparable affinity to the reference inhibitor RVT.
Conclusion

Dihydroxyl Schiff base HNC has been synthesized and characterized successfully using physicochemical and spectroscopic techniques. Attempts to grow the crystal structure of HNC through the slow evaporation of its hot methanolic solution resulted in the formation of its ketoenamine form, denoted as HNC'. The torsion angle of C17:C8:C7:N1 (178.89 ) revealed that the naphthoxide ring is almost coplanar with the azomethine moiety, while the one for C7:N1:C4:C3 (170.77 ) showed that the phenol ring deviates farther from the plane of the azomethine moiety. DFT was used to gain insight into the enolimine-ketoenamine tautomerism of HNC, and it revealed the possibility of HNC' reverting to HNC due to a barrierless transition state of 0.60 kcal/mol obtained between the two tautomers. The stability of each tautomer was brought about by intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions. The calculated HOMO-LUMO gap of HNC is 5.757 eV, suggesting the compound to be moderately chemically reactive. The data from computational investigations suggest that HNC exhibits promising potential as a CDK2 inhibitor, with a docking score of -8.75 kcal/mol, closely approaching the -9.41 kcal/mol of RVT. The validated docking protocol and protein-ligand interaction analysis revealed HNC to be binding firmly to CDK2 through hydrogen bonds (LYS 33, ASP 133) and pi-alkyl/van der Waals interactions, though less diverse than RVT's profile, including a pi-cation bond. The binding free energies (DeltaGtotal) -40.95 kcal/mol and -41.14 kcal/mol for HNC and RVT, respectively, highlighting similar binding affinities for our compound and the known CDK2 inhibitor. While the computational data for this current work unveiled the potential use of HNC as a CDK2 inhibitor, future studies need to be carried out on improving the structural analogs of HNC in order to increase its potency and selectivity against CDK2.
